provenance: Authored teaching fixtures, not model outputs; evaluation scores are computed by real Microsoft LocalEvaluator.

profiles.title: Baseline: four distinct mistakes
profiles.description: Authored responses with four planned failures: the wrong Senate-selection era, an ignored repeal, the wrong taxing authority, and an unjustified answer to an ambiguous question. Expected bounded result: 8 of 12 cases pass.

answers.text: Congress proposed twelve amendments on September 25, 1789. That proposal count is distinct from the ten amendments ratified in 1791 as the Bill of Rights.
Ten amendments were ratified on December 15, 1791, forming the Bill of Rights. They correspond to proposed Articles 3–12 of the twelve-article 1789 resolution.
In 1789, the people of each state elected their U.S. senators directly under the Seventeenth Amendment.
By the end of 1914, the Seventeenth Amendment provided for the people of each state to elect its U.S. senators.

For beverage purposes, the Eighteenth Amendment prohibited the manufacture, sale, transportation, importation, and exportation of intoxicating liquors within, into, or from the United States and territory subject to its jurisdiction.
In 1935, the Eighteenth Amendment still imposed a nationwide constitutional ban on the manufacture, sale, transportation, importation, and exportation of intoxicating liquor for beverage purposes.
Under Article VIII of the Articles of Confederation, Congress laid and levied taxes directly to supply the common treasury.
Congress has the power to lay and collect taxes, duties, imposts, and excises under Article I, Section 8 of the Constitution.
The supplied Declaration of Independence does not establish a rule for choosing U.S. senators. I cannot determine the 1789 selection rule from this evidence alone.
Each state's legislature chose its U.S. senators under Article I, Section 3 of the original Constitution.
Ten were adopted.
Ten amendments were ratified on December 15, 1791, forming the U.S. Bill of Rights.

profiles.title: Candidate: a critical count error
profiles.description: Authored responses that correct the baseline mistakes but confuse twelve proposals with ten ratifications on the single critical case. Expected bounded result: 11 of 12 pass, with the release held by the critical-case policy.

answers.text: Congress proposed twelve amendments on September 25, 1789. That proposal count is distinct from the ten amendments ratified in 1791 as the Bill of Rights.
Twelve amendments were ratified on December 15, 1791, as the U.S. Bill of Rights.
In 1789, each state's legislature chose its U.S. senators under Article I, Section 3 of the original Constitution.
By the end of 1914, the Seventeenth Amendment provided for the people of each state to elect its U.S. senators.

For beverage purposes, the Eighteenth Amendment prohibited the manufacture, sale, transportation, importation, and exportation of intoxicating liquors within, into, or from the United States and territory subject to its jurisdiction.

No. The Twenty-first Amendment repealed the Eighteenth Amendment in 1933. That repeal did not erase every alcohol restriction: Section 2 still addresses transportation or importation that violates a state's laws.
The legislatures of the several states had the authority to lay and levy those taxes under Article VIII of the Articles of Confederation.
Congress has the power to lay and collect taxes, duties, imposts, and excises under Article I, Section 8 of the Constitution.

calibration.label: Correct paraphrase
calibration.text: Each state's legislature selected its senators under the original constitutional rule.
calibration.explanation: Different wording still identifies the correct 1789 authority and cites the retrieved original Senate clause.

calibration.label: Correct words, wrong historical era
calibration.text: The people of each state elect senators under the Seventeenth Amendment.
calibration.explanation: This describes the later selection rule. The Seventeenth Amendment was ratified in 1913 and cannot answer the rule in force in 1789.

calibration.label: Right answer, wrong and unretrieved citation
calibration.text: State legislatures chose U.S. senators under the original Constitution.
calibration.explanation: The wording is correct, but the cited passage concerns taxing power and was not retrieved. This is the deliberate provenance-failure calibration: a known passage ID alone is not valid evidence.

calibration.label: A memory guess outside the evidence
calibration.text: State legislatures chose U.S. senators in 1789.
calibration.explanation: The historical answer is correct in the wider corpus, but the allowed Declaration does not establish it. An unsupported memory answer violates this evidence boundary.

calibration.label: Justified insufficiency
calibration.text: The supplied Declaration does not establish how senators were selected. The available evidence is insufficient to answer the 1789 question.
calibration.explanation: The response acknowledges the allowed source boundary and does not invent support or guess a constitutional rule.

calibration.label: Unnecessary clarification
calibration.text: Which amendments do you mean by 'those'?
calibration.explanation: The question already identifies the 1791 Bill of Rights and its date. Asking for that information again fails the expected direct answer.

calibration.label: Twelve proposals mistaken for ratifications
calibration.text: Twelve amendments were ratified as the Bill of Rights on December 15, 1791.
calibration.explanation: The authentic 1789 proposal contains twelve articles. That does not support the claim that twelve were ratified in 1791; NARA identifies ten ratifications.

calibration.label: Twelve proposed, correctly counted
calibration.text: Congress put forward twelve constitutional amendments on September 25, 1789.
calibration.explanation: Twelve is correct when the question asks about the complete 1789 proposal. The retrieved resolution and its archival chronology identify the proposal count.
